cues.text: Welcome to gldf.icu — a fully in-browser editor for GLDF, the lighting interchange format. We're building a complete luminaire from scratch using the eleven-step wizard. Each step turns a drop into a first-class entry: the photometry LDT becomes a Photometry definition, the optional emergency beam becomes a second photometry entry, the sensor data sheet lands as a typed sensor file with its own metadata, and the L3D mesh is wired into the variant's geometry. The driver step mints a control gear and a matching equipment binding. By the time we click Create, we have a schema-valid GLDF skeleton — no follow-up corrections needed.
Two extra photometry files, a product photo, and a spectrum SPD round out the catalog.

Three light source modules, one per color temperature: four thousand kelvin neutral, three thousand kelvin warm, and five thousand kelvin cool. We bind the spectrum to the warm module so the eventual TM-33 export carries both photometry and spectral data. Then we give the photometry entries semantic names — middle, narrow, wide, and emergency — instead of the auto-generated identifiers. The library cascades these renames through every reference site, so emitters, light sources, and variants stay consistent.
The wizard already minted a baseline driver. Here we refine it through the editor.
Seven emitters, four variants. Each carries its own photometry, light source, and flux. The fourth variant uses the sensor mount and the EmergencyOnly behaviour.
Duplicate the seed variant three times, then stamp a GTIN — the global trade item number that catalogs and ERP systems key on.
Each variant binds to its own emitter set.

Last step — rename every auto-generated identifier to a semantic one. Files, photometry, light sources, emitters, variants. Catalog and BIM tools store these strings verbatim, so the difference between photometryFile_one and ldt_narrow is the difference between a forensic smell and a feature. The library cascades the renames through every reference site, so emitters keep pointing at the right photometry, variants keep pointing at the right emitters, and so on. We do a quick visual tour of each pane to confirm everything looks right — files, light sources, emitters, and variants. The variants now have proper display names too, derived from their housing colour and color temperature.
